qt: to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) Subject:

For the past half-century, the Cyprus issue has been and remains an unresolved regional case of invasion and occupation. It is an infringement of the acquis communautaire and violates the resolutions of the UN Security Council. More active involvement from the EU is essential and important steps are being made in this direction. However, non-EU countries such as Britain, which is closely concerned with the Cyprus issue and the security problem, also need to be more actively involved. In view of this: Is the Commission putting pressure on Britain to do more for the resumption of talks and the pursuit of a fair and viable solution?
at: (English version) to the Commission Loucas Fourlas (PPE) (9 April 2024) Subject: Need for more active involvement of non-EU countries in the Cyprus issue For the past half-century, the Cyprus issue has been and remains an unresolved regional case of invasion and occupation. It is an infringement of the acquis communautaire and violates the resolutions of the UN Security Council. More active involvement from the EU is essential and important steps are being made in this direction. However, non-EU countries such as Britain, which is closely concerned with the Cyprus issue and the security problem, also need to be more actively involved. In view of this: Is the Commission putting pressure on Britain to do more for the resumption of talks and the pursuit of a fair and viable solution? (18 June 2024) The EU’s full commitment to a comprehensive settlement to the Cyprus problem, within the United Nations (UN) framework, in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions and in line with the principles on which the EU is founded and its acquis, has been repeatedly emphasised by the European Council through its Conclusions (1). Most recently, the European Council welcomed the appointment of María Angela Holguín Cuéllar as the UN SecretaryGeneral’s Personal Envoy on Cyprus and stressed the readiness of the EU to play an active role in supporting all stages of the UN-led process (2). The EU works closely with the United Kingdom on many issues and has regular exchanges with British officials on the Cyprus problem as well. The involvement of the United Kingdom, as one of the three guarantor powers, in supporting UN-led efforts towards a comprehensive settlement can only benefit the entire process. However, it is not within the competences of the Commission or any other EU institutions to put pressure on the United Kingdom to do more. The EU continues to look forward to working with the United Kingdom in this regard and on many other issues of joint interest.
